title: The Tokugawa Shogunate
subtitle: Japan's long peace · 1600 – 1868
subject: tokugawa-shogunate
intro: After winning the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, Tokugawa Ieyasu became shogun and ruled Japan from Edo, the future Tokyo. His heirs held power for over 250 years. They kept some 260 daimyo in check through alternate attendance in Edo, banned Christianity, and closed the country to all Europeans except the Dutch at Nagasaki. The long peace brought growing cities, a rich merchant class, kabuki, haiku and ukiyo-e, and Dutch learning. Famine, debt and finally the arrival of Western warships in 1853 undermined the shogunate, which fell to the Meiji Restoration in 1868.

members.note: Founder; kept real power as retired shogun until 1616
First shogun from a branch line (Kii)

events.title: Death of Toyotomi Hideyoshi
events.summary: The unifier of Japan dies leaving a five-year-old heir, Hideyori, under a council of five regents. The most powerful of them, Tokugawa Ieyasu, lord of the rich Kantō plain from his castle at Edo, begins building alliances of his own.

events.title: William Adams reaches Japan
events.summary: The Dutch ship Liefde drifts ashore in Kyushu with a handful of survivors, among them the English pilot William Adams. Ieyasu makes him an adviser on ships and foreign affairs and later a samurai, Miura Anjin — the model for the novel Shōgun.

events.title: Battle of Sekigahara
events.summary: Ieyasu's Eastern Army meets Ishida Mitsunari's Western Army, loyal to the Toyotomi, in a valley in central Japan. Defections in the middle of the battle hand Ieyasu victory; Mitsunari is executed, and the lands of the losing lords are confiscated and redistributed to Tokugawa allies.

events.title: The Tōkaidō and the Five Highways
events.summary: Ieyasu begins organising post stations along the Tōkaidō between Edo and Kyoto, the first of five official highways. Checkpoints watch for 'guns going in and women going out' of Edo, and the roads become arteries of trade, pilgrimage and travel.

events.title: Izumo no Okuni dances the first kabuki
events.summary: A shrine dancer named Okuni performs daring dances on the dry riverbed of the Kamo in Kyoto. Her troupe's style grows into kabuki, which the shogunate later restricts to adult male actors.

events.title: Ieyasu becomes shogun
events.summary: The emperor appoints Tokugawa Ieyasu shogun. He makes the small castle town of Edo his capital and sets daimyo to work building Edo Castle and draining the marshes — the start of the city that becomes Tokyo. Two and a half centuries of peace, the Edo period, begin.

events.title: Ieyasu hands the title to Hidetada
events.summary: After only two years Ieyasu passes the title of shogun to his son Hidetada, making it plain the office is now hereditary in his family. He keeps real power as retired shogun from Sunpu until his death.

events.title: Peace with Korea restored
events.summary: The first Joseon embassy arrives after Hideyoshi's devastating invasions of the 1590s. Twelve Korean missions visit over two centuries, and the Sō clan of Tsushima runs trade with Korea.

events.title: Dutch trading post at Hirado
events.summary: The Dutch East India Company receives a licence from Ieyasu to trade and opens a factory at Hirado. The English follow in 1613 but leave in 1623.

events.title: Satsuma conquers Ryukyu
events.summary: With the shogun's permission, Satsuma invades the Ryukyu Kingdom and makes it a vassal. Ryukyu keeps paying tribute to China, giving Satsuma a hidden channel for Chinese trade — and later wealth to fund the overthrow of the Tokugawa.

events.title: Hasekura's embassy to Spain and Rome
events.summary: Date Masamune, lord of Sendai, sends the samurai Hasekura Tsunenaga across the Pacific to Mexico and on to Madrid and Rome, where he meets the pope. By the time he returns, Christianity is banned and his mission is forgotten.

events.title: Christianity banned
events.summary: Ieyasu orders missionaries expelled and churches destroyed across Japan. Japanese Christians, once some 300,000, are forced to renounce their faith; many are executed, and others worship in secret as 'hidden Christians' for 250 years.

events.title: Sieges of Osaka Castle
events.summary: Ieyasu picks a quarrel with Hideyori and besieges Osaka Castle, defended by tens of thousands of rōnin. A truce lets him fill in the moats; the next summer the castle falls and burns, and Hideyori and his mother Yodo-dono kill themselves. The Toyotomi line ends and no one challenges Tokugawa rule again.

events.title: Laws for the Military Houses
events.summary: The Buke shohatto bind the daimyo: no new castles, no marriages without permission, a single castle per domain. Reissued by each shogun, these rules — together with spies and inspectors — keep some 260 domains in check.

events.title: Death of Ieyasu; the Tōshō-gū
events.summary: Ieyasu dies at Sunpu and is deified as Tōshō Daigongen. His shrine at Nikkō, lavishly rebuilt by his grandson Iemitsu in 1636, becomes a monument to the dynasty.

events.title: Iemitsu becomes shogun
events.summary: The third shogun, the first born to rule rather than win power, completes the Tokugawa system: alternate attendance, the closed country, and tight control of religion.

events.title: Hayashi Razan's Confucian academy
events.summary: The shogun's adviser Hayashi Razan opens a school in Edo. Neo-Confucianism, with its stress on loyalty and a fixed order of samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants, becomes the official philosophy; in 1690 the school moves to the Yushima Seidō.

events.title: Alternate attendance made compulsory
events.summary: Iemitsu's revised Laws for the Military Houses require every daimyo to spend alternate years in Edo and leave his wife and heir there as hostages. The costly processions drain the lords' wealth, bind them to the shogun — and make Edo a vast consumer city.

events.title: Japanese forbidden to go abroad
events.summary: The third of the 'closed country' edicts bans Japanese from travelling overseas on pain of death, and forbids those abroad from returning. Japan's flourishing trading communities in Southeast Asia wither.

events.title: Shimabara Rebellion
events.summary: Famine and savage taxation drive peasants and rōnin of Shimabara and Amakusa, many of them Christian, to revolt under the charismatic teenager Amakusa Shirō. They hold out in the ruined Hara Castle until a huge shogunate army, helped by Dutch cannon, storms it and kills nearly all 37,000 defenders.

events.title: The Portuguese expelled; the country is closed
events.summary: Blaming Catholic influence for Shimabara, the shogunate bans Portuguese ships. When an embassy from Macau comes in 1640 to plead, most of its members are executed. Foreign contact is now limited to the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki, Korea through Tsushima, Ryukyu through Satsuma and the Ainu through Matsumae.

events.title: The Dutch moved to Dejima
events.summary: The Dutch factory is shifted from Hirado to Dejima, a tiny artificial island in Nagasaki harbour. For two centuries it is Japan's window on Europe: the Dutch present annual reports on world news and make a yearly journey to Edo.

events.title: Fall of the Ming
events.summary: The Ming dynasty collapses and the Manchu Qing take Beijing. Ming loyalists appeal to Japan for help, but the shogunate stays out; Chinese junks keep trading at Nagasaki.

events.title: Keian Uprising foiled
events.summary: After Iemitsu's death leaves a ten-year-old shogun, Ietsuna, the strategist Yui Shōsetsu plots a rōnin uprising in Edo. The plot is betrayed, but it pushes the shogunate to ease the confiscations that had created so many masterless samurai.

events.title: Great Fire of Meireki
events.summary: A fire driven by winter winds burns for three days and destroys most of Edo, killing perhaps 100,000 people. The keep of Edo Castle burns and is never rebuilt. The city is replanned with firebreaks, wider streets and temples moved to the edges.

events.title: Shakushain's Revolt
events.summary: The Ainu chief Shakushain leads a rising against the Matsumae domain's unfair trade in Hokkaido. After he is murdered at peace talks the revolt collapses, and Japanese control over the Ainu tightens.

events.title: Mitsui opens its Edo store
events.summary: Mitsui Takatoshi opens the Echigoya drapery in Edo with a revolutionary policy: fixed prices, cash only, and cloth sold by the length. The merchant house grows into a bank and, after 1868, one of the great zaibatsu.

events.title: Tsunayoshi, the 'dog shogun'
events.summary: The fifth shogun, Tsunayoshi, is a scholarly patron of Confucianism, but is remembered for his Edicts on Compassion for Living Things, which made harming dogs a crime and filled Edo with kennels for tens of thousands of strays.

events.title: Genroku culture
events.summary: A wealthy urban culture flowers in Osaka, Kyoto and Edo. Ihara Saikaku writes comic novels of merchant life, Chikamatsu Monzaemon writes plays for the puppet theatre and kabuki, and woodblock ukiyo-e prints show the 'floating world' of theatres and pleasure quarters.

events.title: Bashō sets out on the Narrow Road
events.summary: The poet Matsuo Bashō leaves Edo on a five-month walk through northern Japan. His travel diary Oku no Hosomichi, with its haiku, becomes one of the best-loved works of Japanese literature.

events.title: The forty-seven rōnin take revenge
events.summary: Two years after their lord of Akō was forced to commit suicide for drawing his sword in Edo Castle, his retainers led by Ōishi Yoshio storm the house of the official they blame and kill him. The shogunate orders them to commit seppuku; their story becomes Japan's most famous tale of loyalty, endlessly retold on stage.

events.title: Mount Fuji erupts
events.summary: The Hōei eruption — Fuji's last — follows a giant earthquake and buries farmland under ash; Edo, 100 km away, is darkened. The shogunate levies a special tax for relief, much of which it diverts to its own needs.

events.title: Arai Hakuseki's reforms
events.summary: The Confucian scholar Arai Hakuseki advises the shoguns Ienobu and Ietsugu: he restores the debased coinage, limits the silver and copper draining out through Nagasaki, and interrogates the Italian missionary Sidotti, writing a pioneering study of the West.

events.title: Yoshimune and the Kyōhō Reforms
events.summary: With the main line extinct, Tokugawa Yoshimune of the Kii branch becomes shogun. He cuts spending, raises new rice land, sets up a petition box for commoners and a fire brigade for Edo, and is remembered as the greatest shogun after Ieyasu.

events.title: Ban on Western books eased
events.summary: Yoshimune allows Chinese translations of Western books, apart from Christian ones, to be imported, and has officials learn Dutch. 'Dutch learning' — rangaku — in medicine, astronomy and science begins to grow.

events.title: Dōjima Rice Exchange recognised
events.summary: The shogunate officially licenses the rice market at Dōjima in Osaka, where merchants trade contracts for future delivery of rice — often called the world's first organised futures market. Osaka becomes 'the kitchen of the nation'.

events.title: Kyōhō famine
events.summary: Locusts and cold destroy the rice crop in western Japan; about 12,000 die and Edo sees its first rice riots. Sweet potatoes are promoted as a famine crop.

events.title: The age of Tanuma Okitsugu
events.summary: Under the shogun Ieharu, the chamberlain Tanuma Okitsugu tries to tax commerce, licenses merchant guilds, plans to develop Hokkaido and expand foreign trade. He is accused of corruption and falls after famines and his son's assassination.

events.title: Kaitai Shinsho: Western anatomy in Japanese
events.summary: After watching a dissection that matched a Dutch anatomy book rather than Chinese theory, Sugita Genpaku and his colleagues translate the book. Its publication launches rangaku as a serious scholarly movement.

events.title: Great Tenmei famine
events.summary: Cold summers and the 1783 eruption of Mount Asama cause the worst famine of the era; hundreds of thousands die, especially in the northeast, and riots break out in Edo and Osaka.

events.title: Ienari, the longest-reigning shogun
events.summary: The eleventh shogun Ienari rules for fifty years and fathers over fifty children. His long reign sees both austerity and, later, a lavish and indebted court.

events.title: Kansei Reforms
events.summary: Chief councillor Matsudaira Sadanobu restores austerity, stores rice against famine, cancels samurai debts to merchants, and in 1790 bans 'heterodox' learning at the official academy.

events.title: Russia's first embassy
events.summary: Adam Laxman sails into Nemuro in Hokkaido to return castaways and ask for trade. He is told to go to Nagasaki instead. Russian ships along the northern coasts make coastal defence a growing worry.

events.title: Motoori Norinaga completes the Kojiki-den
events.summary: After 35 years the scholar Motoori Norinaga finishes his commentary on the ancient Kojiki. His 'National Learning' (kokugaku) seeks a pure Japanese spirit before Chinese influence and lays the ground for the cult of the emperor.

events.title: Inō Tadataka maps Japan
events.summary: A retired merchant turned surveyor walks the coasts of Japan for sixteen years. His maps, finished after his death in 1821, are so accurate that the British navy uses copies in the 1860s.

events.title: HMS Phaeton raids Nagasaki
events.summary: A British frigate hunting Dutch ships forces its way into Nagasaki harbour, takes hostages and leaves with supplies. The Nagasaki magistrate commits suicide in shame, and the shogunate tightens coastal defences.

events.title: Edict to repel foreign ships
events.summary: Alarmed by British whalers landing for supplies, the shogunate orders any foreign ship approaching the coast to be driven off by force, without question.

events.title: The Siebold incident
events.summary: Philipp Franz von Siebold, the German doctor at Dejima who taught Western medicine to Japanese students, is caught trying to take forbidden maps of Japan out of the country. He is expelled and several of his Japanese contacts are punished.

events.title: Hokusai's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji
events.summary: Katsushika Hokusai, in his seventies, publishes the series that includes The Great Wave off Kanagawa. Hiroshige's Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō follows in 1833–34. Later exported to Europe, these prints inspire Monet, Van Gogh and the Impressionists.

events.title: Ōshio Heihachirō's rising in Osaka
events.summary: During the Tenpō famine, the former police official and Confucian scholar Ōshio Heihachirō sells his books to feed the poor, then leads an armed rising against officials and rice hoarders. It is quickly crushed but a quarter of Osaka burns — a shock that a shogunate official should rebel.

events.title: The Morrison incident
events.summary: An American merchant ship bringing home Japanese castaways is fired on and driven away under the repel edict. Critics such as the rangaku scholars who protest are punished.

events.title: Tenpō Reforms
events.summary: Mizuno Tadakuni tries a last round of austerity: merchant guilds dissolved, luxuries and popular fiction banned, peasants sent back from Edo to the land. The reforms fail and Mizuno is dismissed, exposing the shogunate's weakness.

events.title: News of China's defeat
events.summary: Reports of Britain's victory in the Opium War alarm Edo. The repel edict is replaced with orders to give foreign ships fuel and water, and some domains begin casting Western-style cannon.

events.title: Perry's Black Ships
events.summary: Commodore Matthew Perry arrives in Edo Bay with four warships and demands that Japan open its ports. The shogunate, unable to resist, signs the Convention of Kanagawa the next year — the beginning of the end of the closed country.

events.title: Harris Treaty
events.summary: Ii Naosuke signs a commercial treaty with the United States without the emperor's consent, opening ports to trade and granting extraterritoriality. The 'unequal treaties' and the court's opposition turn many samurai against the shogunate.
events.wiki: Treaty of Amity and Commerce (United States–Japan)

events.title: Ii Naosuke assassinated
events.summary: The shogunate's chief minister is cut down outside Edo Castle by samurai who oppose his treaties and purges. Its authority never recovers.

events.title: Satsuma and Chōshū ally
events.summary: The two great southwestern domains, both outside the Tokugawa inner circle since Sekigahara, secretly agree to work together against the shogunate. Months later Chōshū defeats a shogunate army.

events.title: The last shogun returns power
events.summary: Tokugawa Yoshinobu hands his governing authority back to the emperor, hoping to keep a leading role in a new council of lords.

events.title: Imperial rule restored; the shogunate abolished
events.summary: Satsuma and allied troops seize the palace in Kyoto and the young emperor proclaims the restoration of imperial rule. The Boshin War follows; Edo Castle is handed over without a fight in May, and becomes the Imperial Palace. After 265 years, Tokugawa rule is over.
